summary: The Animal mortality rate calculator turns the available stock, number of animals sold and more into number of deaths. It suits an animal, a plant or a biological process whose scale you want to put into perspective. Nothing is submitted anywhere: the arithmetic runs in the page you are looking at.

sections.title: How does the Animal mortality rate calculator work?
sections.html:
The Animal mortality rate calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports number of deaths in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the available stock, number of animals sold, the mortality rate and the cumulative mortality.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Animal mortality rate calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Number of deaths=-closing stock − number of animals sold + number of newborns + opening stock
Opening stock=-number of newborns + number of deaths ÷ mortality rate
Closing stock=number of deaths ÷ cumulative mortality
Case mortality=number of deaths from disease ÷ number of disease cases
Number of newborns=available stock − opening stock

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Animal mortality rate calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Comparing two organisms, populations or processes
  • Supporting a lesson, a lecture or a field note
  • Putting a biological quantity into a scale you can picture
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the available stock, number of animals sold and the mortality rate — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Animal mortality rate calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns number of deaths, derived from the available stock, number of animals sold and the mortality rate. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Animal mortality rate calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the available stock, number of animals sold, the mortality rate and the cumulative mortality, which is 6 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter mortality rate in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Mortality rate opens in percent and the chip beside it offers 6 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: Is the Animal mortality rate calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
